questions.q: What is the difference between a conceptual interview question and a tool-specific one, according to this lesson?
options: A conceptual question tests understanding of a tradeoff independent of any one screen; a tool-specific question tests whether you've actually operated a specific Tableau feature
Conceptual questions are always easier than tool-specific ones
Tool-specific questions only apply to Tableau Public, never Server or Cloud
There is no real difference — interviewers ask only one type
questions.explain: The lesson describes conceptual questions (like relationships vs. joins vs. blends) as testing understanding of tradeoffs, while tool-specific questions (like walking through a publish workflow) test hands-on operation of the actual tool.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend publishing the three Chapter 17 projects to Tableau Public specifically?
options: Because Tableau Public is free and fully public, making it the right home for a portfolio a hiring manager can open with no login required
Because Tableau Public is the only place workbooks can include parameters
Because Tableau Server cannot host dashboards with LOD expressions
Because Tableau Public requires a paid enterprise license
questions.explain: Lesson 87 established that Tableau Public trades privacy for being free and open — exactly the tradeoff that makes it the right destination for a public job-search portfolio.

questions.q: What distinguishes a strong resume bullet, according to this lesson's guidance?
options: It describes something concrete and provable, like specific techniques used in a real built project, rather than a generic skill claim
It lists as many Tableau features as possible in one sentence
It avoids naming any specific project or technique
It should always be exactly one word, like "Tableau"
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts a generic claim like 'Proficient in Tableau' with a specific, defensible bullet describing an actual project and its techniques — something you can back up in an interview because you actually built it.

questions.q: What is the purpose of preparing both a '30-second version' and a '3-minute version' of a project pitch?
options: Different interview moments call for different lengths — a quick one-liner versus a full walkthrough with a live demo
The 30-second version replaces the need to ever demo the project live
Interviewers only ever want the 3-minute version
The two versions describe two different projects, not the same one
questions.explain: The lesson recommends rehearsing both a short, high-level pitch and a longer full walkthrough with a live demo, since interviews call for different depths at different moments.

questions.q: According to the lesson's closing section, what actually separates a finished course from a finished career step?
options: Having real, working, explainable projects that combine everything learned — not just having completed individual lessons
Receiving a printed certificate of completion
Memorizing every calculated field syntax taught in the course
Watching all 95 lessons without doing any of the labs
questions.explain: The lesson states plainly that the three Chapter 17 projects — real, working, and explainable — are what separate a finished course from a finished career step, not a certificate or passive viewing.
